question:
What word does Chaucer NOT make a rhyme with in Book of the Duchess?

Answer Choices:
A. Wente
B. Here
C. Fool
D. Hool
E. Countour
F. None of the above

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Hool — The key is whether the word actually occupies a rhyme position. In Book of the Duchess, “hool” occurs only inside a line, not as the end-word of a paired couplet, so Chaucer does not make a rhyme with it. By contrast, “wente” is paired with “entente,” “here” with “spere,” and “countour” with “governour”; those are functioning rhyme words. That makes Hool the odd one out.

In the rhyme-royal octaves of the *Book of the Duchess* Chaucer regularly uses
wente ~ sente / kente, here ~ there / fere / dere, fool ~ cool / tool and the
Middle-English form hool ~ fool / hool ‘whole’. The rare professional noun
countour / counteur ‘counter, reckoner’ is attested in Chaucer’s vocabulary
elsewhere but it never occurs in a rhyming position in the *Duchess*, so it is
the item of the list that does not function as a rhyme-word in that poem.

In the Middle-English rhyming couplets of the *Book of the Duchess* Chaucer regularly uses the four
rime-words you list. *wente* is the normal past of *gān* and is rhymed with *schente/mente* etc.,
*here* is rhymed with *there/were* etc., *fool* is rhymed with the Middle English *hool* ~ *hol*
‘whole, hale’ and the two forms are used as a conventional fool/hool rime-pair in the dream-
vision. The noun *countour* ‘counter, reckoner’ is not employed as a rime-word in the *Duchess*;
it is a later Chaucerian loan and does not occur in a rhyming position in that early dream-vision.

countour that is the non-rhyming item. If the orthographic variant hoole = hool
is identified with the whole-rhyme the poem does in fact rhyme with every
item on the list, i.e. in effect None of the above.
